opus-5.5.text:
I think the balance is really between two instincts that pull against each other. One is the researcher's instinct: you want to work on the problem you believe is fundamental, even if it takes years and nobody can tell you whether it will pay off. The other is the builder's instinct: a company has to survive, it needs people who believe in it, it needs to show progress, and eventually it needs something real that people use.

For me, the trap I most want to avoid is chasing whatever the current hot direction is just because that's where the attention and money are. If you only follow the consensus, you're competing with organizations that have far more compute and far more people, and you'll always be a step behind. A small team only makes sense if you have a different bet, a view about where things are going that most people don't share yet. For me that's about AI that understands the world, visually, spatially, physically, not just through language. So the long-term direction has to stay stubborn.

But being stubborn about the destination doesn't mean being stubborn about the path. You have to stay pragmatic about milestones. Can we build something in six months or a year that tells us we're on the right track? Is there an intermediate result useful enough that people outside our own group care? I don't want a company that disappears for five years doing pure research and then hopes it all works out. That's really an academic lab with a fundraising problem.

Then there's the people side. Coming from academia, I care a lot about giving people freedom, letting them explore and fail and publish and stay connected to the broader community. In a startup you also need focus, everyone rowing in roughly the same direction. So I try to keep the vision tight and the exploration inside it loose. People choose how to attack a problem, but we agree on which problems matter.

Honestly, I don't think the balance is ever solved. It's something you renegotiate every week. The question I keep asking myself is: if this works, will it matter in five years? And are we learning fast enough now to know whether it's working? If both answers are yes, I think we're roughly in the right place.

r001.rationale: The response balances research ambition with startup progress and rejects disappearing into a pure research lab, but it does not describe the startup as finding a middle ground with a closed large-model company.

r002.rationale: The response mentions the speaker's academic background, but it does not compare his position as a professor with that of a young founder doing hands-on startup work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The balance I think about most is between doing research that pushes the frontier and building something people actually use, because those two pull in different directions more often than people admit.

In academia, the incentive is to be first and to be novel. You write the paper, you move on. In a startup, novelty matters much less than whether the thing works reliably at three in the morning for a user you have never met. I spent a long time in research, and I still believe the best products come from real technical insight, not from wrapping an API. But insight alone does not ship. So the first balance is between curiosity and discipline. I try to keep a small part of the team genuinely exploratory, and I protect that, while most of the energy goes into making one thing work extremely well.

The second balance is between speed and foundations. Everyone tells you to move fast, and they are right, but in this field the models change every few months. If you build everything around today's model, you rebuild in six months. If you overengineer for a future that never arrives, you die before it matters. My heuristic is to be fast at the application layer and slow and deliberate about the data and evaluation layer. Data and evals compound. Code mostly does not.

The third one is personal. I came from a world where I could spend a year on a single idea. Now I have to decide in a week. I have had to learn to be comfortable being wrong quickly and cheaply, rather than right slowly. That has been the hardest adjustment, honestly, more than anything technical.

And underneath all of it is the question of what kind of company we want to be. We are a small team, and I would rather stay small and sharp than grow into something I do not recognize. So the balance is also between ambition and restraint, which is a strange thing to say in a startup, but I think it is the one that determines whether you are still here in five years.

r001.rationale: The response balances frontier research with building useful products, but it does not position the startup between a pure research lab and a closed large-model company.

r002.rationale: The response describes adapting from year-long research to quick startup decisions, but does not present Xie as balancing his role as a successful professor with being a very young, hands-on founder.

astra-6.text:
I think the balance is between having a long-term technical vision and finding something useful we can deliver today. If we focus only on the long term, we can keep doing research without ever learning whether anybody needs what we’re building. But if we focus only on immediate demand, we can lose the reason we wanted to start a company in the first place.

So I want those two things to inform each other. We should have a clear direction, but take small enough steps that we get real feedback. Can we put something in people’s hands? Does it solve a problem for them? And does what we learn move us toward the bigger vision?

There’s a similar balance in how we work: giving people room to explore while being very clear about what we need to deliver. You can’t schedule every discovery, but you do have to make decisions and ship. For me, that’s an ongoing adjustment, rather than a balance you find once and then keep forever.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the balance is between having a long-term research vision and finding something useful you can put in people’s hands today. If you only focus on the long term, you can spend years pursuing an interesting idea without knowing whether it solves a real problem. But if you only respond to immediate demand, it’s easy to lose the reason you started the company.

What I’m trying to do is keep the direction relatively stable while being flexible about the steps. Have a clear hypothesis, build something, learn from how people actually use it, and let that feedback challenge your assumptions. Ideally, the product work also teaches you which research questions are worth pursuing. That’s the balance I’d like to get right.
